questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: English idioms and expressions that use the word 'bee'
How to keep bees in your own back garden
Falling bee numbers and new ways to pollinate crops
Why honey is becoming more expensive in the shops
questions.why: They discuss bees declining, the risk to food, and solutions like pollinating with drones.

questions.q: How much of the food we eat depends on insects to pollinate crops?
options: One third
One half
One quarter
Almost all of it
questions.why: Neil says one third of the food we eat depends on insects to pollinate crops.

questions.q: What is happening to bees in some European countries?
options: Their numbers are rising quickly
They are moving to warmer countries
They are being replaced by other insects
Up to half of bee species face extinction
questions.why: Sam says in some European countries up to half of all bee species are facing extinction.

questions.q: According to Claire Bates, how are crops like wheat, rice and corn pollinated?
options: By bees
By the wind
By farmers by hand
By birds
questions.why: She says some staple crops such as wheat, rice and corn are pollinated by the wind.

questions.q: How do bees carry pollen from flower to flower?
options: They store it in their hive
They eat it and release it later
It sticks to them as they collect nectar
They carry it in their mouths
questions.why: Claire Bates says as they collect nectar to eat, pollen sticks to them.

questions.q: What problem with bees does Keren Mimran describe?
options: They often sting the farm workers in the fields
You can't control them, e.g. they stay in when it rains
They are too expensive for most farmers to buy
They only visit certain flowers and ignore crops
questions.why: She says we can't control their behaviour: they don't leave the hive in rain or heavy wind.

questions.q: What has Keren Mimran's company developed?
options: A new type of bee
A chemical to protect bees
Hives that work in bad weather
Drones that drop pollen on orchards
questions.why: Sam says her company has developed drones to drop pollen on her orchard.

questions.q: What does the need for high-tech solutions show, according to Neil?
options: How serious the pollination problem is for food
That bees are no longer needed on modern farms
That technology is always better than nature
That most farmers dislike working with bees
questions.why: Neil says the need for them reflects the seriousness of the pollination problem for food security.
